summary: Mail delivery looks for an MX record and falls back to an A/AAAA record, even when a domain accepts no mail. This document defines a Null MX record that explicitly says a domain accepts no mail, so senders can stop right away instead of trying.

eli5.summary: This is a sign on a house saying: no mail delivered here. Senders see it and do not wait around trying.

questions: how to say a domain accepts no email
what is a null mx record
how to publish a null mx
subtitle: A single MX record that tells the world a domain accepts no email, so senders give up at once.

tldr.problem: When a domain has no MX record, mail senders fall back to its A or AAAA address and keep retrying, typically for a week, even if nothing there accepts mail.
tldr.mechanism: The domain publishes exactly one MX record with preference 0 and the root label ('.') as the mail exchanger, which means no mail server exists for the domain.
tldr.outcome: Senders can fail delivery on the first attempt and receivers can reject mail quickly, with no dedicated SMTP listener needed.

facts.label: Records allowed
facts.value: A null MX must be the only MX

today: RFC 7505 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the null MX record.

sections.title: Why a Domain Needs to Say No Mail
sections.content:
An SMTP client finds a mail server for a domain in a set order, described in Section 5 of RFC 5321. It first looks up the domain's MX records. If there are none, it falls back to the domain's A or AAAA records. That overloads an address record, whose main job is something else, with a mail meaning.

So a domain with no MX records still gets delivery attempts to its web or other hosts. If nothing listens for SMTP there, the sending Mail Transfer Agent (MTA) tries again and again, typically for a week, before giving up. The sender is told late about misdirected mail and wastes resources in the meantime.

The RFC defines the No Service MX, informally called null MX, so that all delivery attempts fail immediately without the domain running an SMTP listener just to refuse mail.
sections.eli5: If a house has no mailbox, the mail carrier might keep coming back for a week to check. A null MX is a clear note on the door that says do not bother.

sections.title: The Null MX Record
sections.content:
A domain that accepts no email publishes a single MX record (defined in Section 3.3.9 of RFC 1035). Its data holds preference number 0 and a zero-length label as the exchange domain, written . in master files. That means there is no mail exchanger for the domain.

Because . is not a valid host name, a null MX cannot be mistaken for an ordinary MX record. The idea is modeled on the SRV record from RFC 2782, where a . target has a similar meaning of no service available.

A domain that advertises a null MX MUST NOT advertise any other MX record.
sections.eli5: The record points to a mail server whose name is just a dot, which is not a real name at all. That is the way of saying: there is no mail server here.

sections.title: What Happens When Mail Meets a Null MX
sections.content:
Mistyped addresses are common, such as alice@www.example.com, alice@example.org or alice@examp1e.com instead of alice@example.com. With a null MX, the mail system can report the failure when the user sends the message, rather than hours or days later. An SMTP client learns on its first attempt that the address is undeliverable, so it avoids queuing and retries.

Abusers often forge return addresses that cannot receive mail. A null MX lets Delivery Status Notifications (DSNs) and other replies to such mail be disposed of efficiently. A receiving server that rejects mail from an undeliverable sender domain can also be more confident that a later DSN to a real sender will reach a working server.

When a submission or relay server rejects a recipient because of a null MX, it SHOULD use reply code 556 (from RFC 7504) and enhanced status code 5.1.10. When a server rejects mail because the sender's domain has a null MX, it SHOULD use reply code 550 and enhanced status code 5.7.27.
sections.eli5: If you address a letter to a house with the no-mail sign, the post office hands it straight back to you today. You do not wait a week to find out.

sections.title: Domains That Send Mail
sections.content:
Null MX is meant mainly for domains that neither send nor receive mail, but still get mail because of mistakes or malice. Many receivers reject mail with an invalid return address, and an invalid return address often signals spam. So mail systems SHOULD NOT publish a null MX for domains they use in RFC5321.MailFrom or RFC5322.From addresses. If they do, their mail risks being rejected.

Operators of domains that send no mail can also publish Sender Policy Framework (SPF) -all policies (RFC 7208) to declare that. Null MX does not replace the null reverse-path of Section 4.5.5 of RFC 5321 and does not change how that is used.
sections.eli5: Do not put the no-mail sign on a house you send letters from. People who get a letter with a no-return-address house on it may toss it out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Inside the DNS, a null MX is an ordinary MX record, so it adds no new security issues. If wanted, it can be secured like any other DNS record using DNSSEC.
sections.eli5: The sign is written in the same ink as every other DNS record, so it can be protected the same way.

sections.title: New Enhanced Status Codes
sections.content:
IANA added two entries to the Enumerated Status Codes subregistry of the SMTP Enhanced Status Codes registry. Code X.1.10 (sample text: Recipient address has null MX) goes with basic status code 556 and is returned when an address is marked invalid by a null MX.

Code X.7.27 (sample text: Sender address has null MX) goes with basic status code 550. It is returned when the sender address has a null MX and the SMTP receiver is configured to reject mail from such senders, for example because it could not return a DSN.
sections.eli5: Two new error labels were added to the official list, one for mail sent to a no-mail domain and one for mail claiming to come from one.
